meeting_header:
Date: 2025-07-21
Time: 09:23 - 10:31 PT
Duration: 68 minutes
Attendees: Samira (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Maya (Redwood Infra), Jordan (Redwood Solutions); Rajiv (Aurelia ML Infra), Laura (Aurelia SRE), Tom (Aurelia CTO), Priya (Aurelia Data Ops)
summary: Technical deep dive focusing on GPU runtime behavior across kernel selection paths, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM tradeoffs, CUDA graph stability, persistent KV cache eviction patterns, batching strategies, and quantization impacts. Agreed to run customer-specific traces and scheduled a bench day to validate eviction-aware batching with their 13B model in VPC/on-prem context. Action items assigned for traces, prompt sets, config diffs, and POC pricing.
topics: kernel selection heuristics; TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM throughput-latency profiles; CUDA-graphs instability and warmup; persistent KV cache sizing and eviction; batching windows and tail latency; quantization (4-bit vs 8-bit) quality tradeoffs; VPC/on-prem network egress and pinning GPUs; canary rollouts for model variants.
transcript:
00:00 Samira (AE): ok uh hi everyone thanks for joining on a Monday morning, let's do quick intros — from Redwood we have Diego, Maya and Jordan, and from Aurelia we have Rajiv, Laura, Tom and Priya. We're hoping to walk through kernel-level observations and make sure our svc matches your on-prem constraints.

00:45 Rajiv (ML Infra): yeah thanks, appreciate it. main ask is: our inference cost is spiking on long-context prompts and we're seeing weird eviction behavior in the KV cache — sometimes latencies jump 2-3x. we want to know if that's a kernel scheduling problem or batch sizing or something like CUDA-graphs flushing.

01:15 Diego (SE): totally — and quick note, when you say eviction do you mean the LRU eviction in the prefix/KV cache? or are you talking host-GPU memory thrash?

01:40 Rajiv: mostly GPU-side KV eviction. we have persistent cache on the GPU but when we get concurrent long sessions it looks like the cache entries get evicted and then recomputed, so token cost spikes.

02:10 Maya (Infra): one hypothesis is the persistent KV allocation plus CUDA-graph replay — if the exec path switches kernels (like fused-attn vs unfused) the graph can recompile or re-alloc which makes the runtimes evict. also alignment of sequence length distribution matters.

02:45 Laura (SRE): can you say a bit more about "exec path switch"? we use Triton in prod today and we thought once the graph is compiled it's stable.

03:10 Diego: yeah with Triton or TRT-LLM there's usually a preferred kernel for a given head-dim/seq-len combo. with vLLM's approach the runtime sometimes selects different microkernels at runtime based on requests, and that can lead to cache misses in CUDA-graphs. also some kernels require different temporary buffers which pushes memory pressure.

03:48 Tom (CTO): are we talking about model-level quantization too? we were experimenting with 4-bit and saw quality drop for some outputs. would that interact with kernel choice?

04:12 Maya: it can. quantized kernels may use different matmul/code paths optimized for int4/8. those kernels sometimes have different memory layout and tiling which changes cache pressure. We saw on a 13B that switching from 8-bit to 4-bit saved ~30% token cost but increased tail-latency variance by ~25% in our microbench.

04:45 Rajiv: that's consistent with us — cost down but jitter up. so question is: with Redwood's runtime do you prefer TRT-LLM or vLLM for our workload?

05:10 Diego: short answer: depends on your SLOs. TRT-LLM gives great peak throughput and lower steady-state latency for fixed shapes — if you can pin sequence length and don't need large variety of prompts. vLLM is better if you have varied prompt shapes and want dynamic batching and prefix caching optimizations. for eviction concerns, we have a hybrid routing that prefers persistent-kv friendly kernels.

05:48 Rajiv: hybrid routing? please explain that — is that something in the open-source runtime or product-only?

06:05 Diego: it's a Redwood inference runtime feature — we maintain kernel profiles per model+shape and route requests to a kernel-path that balances latency vs memory pressure. e.g., we can route small interactive requests to low-latency kernels and large batch jobs to throughput-optimized kernels. the routing can be policy-driven — cost-first or latency-first.

06:42 Priya (Data Ops): from compliance perspective, we need everything within our VPC and no external egress. does any of the kernel tracing require outbound telemetry?

06:58 Samira: no — all kernel traces we share for POC can be collected in your VPC and sanitized. Diego will provide the CUPTI/NVTX capture instructions. we can take the tarball from you and we process it offline.

07:20 Diego: we'll also share a small test harness script — it's in the bench sheet — that reproduces the eviction pattern. note: when capturing traces please run with small warmup (20 steps) and then steady run (100 samples). avoid using perf samples on the same run because it can skew timings.

08:05 Laura: ok got it, we'll try to collect traces. what about CUDA-graphs? we've seen graphs crash on our older gen GPUs after a few thousand replays. any known fixes?

08:30 Maya: yes we've seen instability tied to certain fused attention kernels in specific CUDA versions. workaround 1: disable graph capture for that code path and use persistent exec with manual batching; workaround 2: pin to a GPU driver/CUDA patch where graph replays are stable. we can check your driver version and recommend minimal upgrades.

09:05 Tom: any risk to throughput if we disable CUDA-graphs?

09:22 Diego: slight drop in peak throughput for repeated identical sequences but can reduce tail volatility. sometimes it's better to accept a 5-10% throughput hit to avoid 2x tail spikes.

09:50 Rajiv: curious about the kernel selection process — do you do autotuning on first deploy? how do you decide math kernel vs fused kernel?

10:10 Maya: we run a per-model microbench during onboarding. it probes shapes and runs small matmul/attention permutations; the runtime picks the fastest stable kernel and records that in a profile. we keep fallbacks and also a quick live probe if we detect a pattern change. it's not perfect — there are tradeoffs between compile time and stability.

10:45 Priya: and what about quantization quality checks? can we do automated evals?

11:05 Jordan (Solutions): yes, Redwood Optimize can run your eval set against multiple quant streams (8-bit, 4-bit, and mixed) and produce quality regression alerts. we tie those alerts to rollouts so you don't ship a worse quantized model by accident.

11:30 Rajiv: that sounds useful. can you add our prompt set to that pipeline?

11:40 Jordan: absolutely — that's part of the POC scope if you want it.

12:05 Laura: let's get to some concrete numbers — for a 13B model with 4k context on an A100, what's a ballpark of tokens/sec for TRT-LLM vs vLLM? we have mostly medium-length interactive sessions (avg seq len ~512).

12:35 Diego: for the 13B with 512 avg, TRT-LLM tuned kernels showed ~950-1150 tokens/sec under sustained load with large batches; vLLM with dynamic batching saw ~600-900 tokens/sec but lower median latency for small requests. again numbers vary based on quant and KV hit rate. with persistent KV hit-rate >85% vLLM can match or exceed TRT in median latencies.

13:18 Rajiv: what about if KV hit-rate drops to 50%?

13:30 Diego: then vLLM becomes more expensive per-token because you recompute prefixes. TRT-LLM's advantage in dense matmuls shines, especially if the kernel is fused and has lower mem copies. so eviction behavior matters a lot.

13:58 Tom: so practically we need to measure our actual KV hit curves. Rajiv will collect that?

14:05 Rajiv: yes we can. we'll export a 24hr sample of KV hits and miss latencies and attach.

14:20 Maya: great — also include your GPU driver and kernel versions, and whether you're using MIG or not. MIG can change scheduler behavior.

14:45 Diego: another note on batching: we support eviction-aware batching where we constrain batch composition to avoid introducing new prefix lengths that will evict entries. that reduces effective batch sizes a bit but reduces tail.

15:10 Laura: is that a tradeoff we can tune live? can we set a percent of latency-first traffic?

15:25 Diego: yes — routing policies allow you to declare routes with 'latency_slo' and 'cost_sensitivity', and the runtime applies different batching windows and kernel-paths per route.

15:55 Rajiv: quick Q on VPC/on-prem: our security team is concerned about firmware and KMS integration. if we move to private deployment, what's Redwood's model for KMS?

16:15 Samira: for Private we support customer-managed KMS (CloudHSM or on-prem HSM) and keys never leave your network. we can sign artifacts inside your VPC; our control plane can be air-gapped if needed. we'll share the security packet with details.

16:40 Priya: thanks. also we have an older cluster with T4s mixed with A100s — how bad is heterogenous hardware for kernel routing?

16:58 Maya: heterogenous fleets complicate kernel selection; the runtime will select kernels compatible with the least-capable device in a pool unless you tag pools by GPU type. best practice: separate pools by GPU class, or use routing rules to prefer A100 for high-throughput routes.

17:25 Tom: back to CUDA-graphs, do you have examples where graphs cause memory leaks?

17:42 Diego: yes in older CUDA 11.x there were leak patterns in certain cuBLAS fused kernels when replay count exceeded a threshold; we have fixes in newer drivers. if you can't upgrade, disabling capture on those kernels is safer.

18:05 Rajiv: let's discuss the bench day — what will Redwood bring vs what we should prepare?

18:20 Samira: Redwood brings a small harness, kernel-level tracing scripts (CUPTI/NVTX), comparison runner for TRT-LLM and vLLM, and a suggested config for eviction-aware batching. Aurelia should provide model artifacts, tokenization sample, and access to a test GPU instance in your VPC (we can supply AMIs).

18:50 Rajiv: understood. we'll provision a node next week.

19:12 Diego: one more nuance — when using quantization, watch out for activation scaling and outlier embedding tokens; sometimes a small subspace of tokens triggers large softmax values and the 4-bit quant can clamp those causing hallucination-like artifacts. we recommend running the eval set to detect these cases.

19:47 Laura: ok, good to know. how fast can you run the Optimize eval? hours? days?

20:00 Jordan: depends on set size — 1k examples can run in a few hours; full regression sets may take 24-48 hours. we'll prioritize top-200 prompts for the POC.

20:25 Tom: any legal or procurement blockers for on-prem deployment we should be aware of?

20:40 Samira: standard enterprise MSA and an addendum for on-prem deployment; we have an SOC-2 package; for very regulated environments we do an onsite review. legal and procurement usually take 4-6 weeks.

21:05 Rajiv: ok that's fine. let's talk briefly about fallback policies — if we run out of capacity on your private pool, can Redwood route to hosted fallback?

21:25 Diego: yes that's supported but it depends on contract and data residency constraints. failover can route to a dedicated cold-pool inside your region; we can encrypt payloads and ensure no retention in hosted fallback. it requires an explicit fallback agreement.

21:55 Priya: can we get a sample fallback config?

22:05 Samira: yes we'll send a sample routing YAML with canary/failover rules.

22:30 Rajiv: a couple of quick technical asks for Diego: 1) capture a small trace showing how you detect kernel path change, 2) example of flamegraph that links to kernel names, and 3) sample config for eviction-aware batching.

22:55 Diego: yep we'll do 1-3. expect uploads to our secure S3 share (or you can host within your VPC if preferred).

23:20 Laura: last question: what's the expected uplift if we increase persistent KV to hold 90% of active prefixes versus current 60%?

23:40 Diego: back-of-envelope: if persistent KV stores 90% hot prefixes you avoid recomputing prefix attention about 30-40% of the time for your workload; that typically reduces tokens/sec cost by ~20-30% and reduces tail by ~35%. exact numbers depend on your prompt distribution.

24:05 Tom: great. any pitfalls around quant + persistent KV? can quantized KV caches degrade when mixing precisions?

24:30 Maya: yes mixing precisions in KV cache is messy; we recommend storing KV in native float16 on GPU even if model weights are 4-bit quant — this preserves numeric stability in attention. that costs memory but pays off in stability.

24:55 Rajiv: good call. ok let's wrap with concrete next steps and owners.

25:10 Samira: recap — Redwood to share POC pricing and routing YAML (Samira). Diego to produce CUPTI/NVTX capture guide + first kernel traces (Diego). Maya to provide minimal driver/CUDA recommendations (Maya). Rajiv to provide model artifacts and sample prompts (Rajiv). schedule bench day once traces confirm the pattern.

25:45 Rajiv: thanks all. we'll aim to have artifacts by Thursday.

26:00 Tom: appreciate the deep dive, useful pointers.

26:12 Samira: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with the action items and links.

01:08:00 [call end note]: meeting ended, recording stopped.
